EICMA 2026 • Honda Has a Taste of the e-MTB World with the RN0 Motor-Assisted Bicycle
Owner Bought This 2024 Mercedes-Maybach, Drove 286 Miles and Never Touched It Again
25 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
Keeping a car as low mileage as possible can be part of the owner’s plan to cash in at some point. However, this is definitely not the case. The original owner bought this Mercedes-Maybach S 580 back in 2024, drove 286 miles, and parked it. Now, the luxury sedan has just hit the market.
The original owner of this 2024 Mercedes-Maybach S 580 4MATIC paid $225,550, with over $22,000 worth of options back in 2024. Two years later, the car is listed for sale with just 286 miles on the clock and a two-owner background. Just weeks after he purchased the car, serious health issues occurred.
So he parked the car and tended to them. Soon after, because his medical condition no longer allowed him to drive, he lost his license. So a year later, he had to change the registration to his son in order to satisfy the insurance company.
The son doesn’t really need the Maybach, so it has been listed for sale as a two-year-old, very low-mileage luxury vehicle. The sedan is finished in a two-tone paint scheme, with Selenite Grey for the upper section and Cirrus Silver Lower for the lower section, over Macchiato and Bronze Brown Pearl Exclusive Maybach Nappa leather.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The model rides on 21-inch Maybach Exclusive forged wheels, the so-called champagne-flute wheels because the spaces between their slim, polished spokes are shaped like tall, narrow champagne glasses radiating out from the center cap. The wheels are wrapped in Pirelli P Zero tires.
The Maybach left the Sindelfingen factory with the Executive Rear Seat Package Plus, the $6,000 optional upgrade that converts the standard five-seat cabin into a private four-seat first-class lounge. The rear passengers sit in executive seats with recline, memory, and massaging functions.
Heated and ventilated massaging front seats, heated and ventilated rear Executive seats, and a four-zone automatic climate control are also on board , under the panoramic glass sunroof and behind the soft-close doors.
The refrigerator out back houses Maybach champagne flutes and champagne flute holders in typical Maybach fashion. The original owner surely specced this car the right way. He chose the Driver Assistance Package, the Active Distance Assist Distronic, and the 360-degree surround-view camera.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Active Parking Assist sensors, a toll gate transponder, heated power-folding side mirrors, and the LED Intelligent Light System with Adaptive Highbeam Assist are also on the menu. The car sits on the Airmatic air suspension and features rear-axle steering.
The driver controls most of the functions via the 12.8-inch OLED touchscreen running the MBUX system with navigation. A 12.3-inch configurable digital instrument panel and a head-up display provide the relevant driving data.
The Burmester 4D Surround Sound System provides the soundtrack on board. The alternative soundtrack is the V8 orchestra coming from under the hood. However, considering the insulation of the Maybach’s cabin, the twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8, mated to a 48-volt mild-hybrid Integrated Starter Generator, is not exactly an audible soundtrack.
It is better at pushing the car forward rather than providing entertainment, with the force of 496 horsepower (503 metric horsepower and 516 pound-feet (700 Newton meters) of torque. That is enough for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 4.3 seconds and a top speed electronically limited at 155 mph (250 kph). A nine-speed 9G-Tronic automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners with the help of the 4MATIC all-wheel-drive system.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Even at this kind of ultra-low mileage , the two-year-old Maybach isn’t flawless. There is a stone chip below the left headlight, and the 48-volt battery module was replaced under warranty in January 2026. However, the vehicle comes with a clean Carfax with no accidents or mileage discrepancies. No surprise there…
The Maybach is being auctioned off on Bring a Trailer. After two days online, with five days left to go, bidding is still light-years away from the sticker price. The most generous offer reached $77,777, but there is still time. The future owner is getting the window sticker, the owner’s manual, service records, and a clean California title in the current owner's name.
However, the future owner will have to deal with a major issue. In October 2026, Mercedes-Benz issued a major safety recall affecting the 2024 Mercedes-Maybach S 580 due to front brake hoses that can rupture and leak brake fluid. The recall affects 30,064 Mercedes-Benz S-Class, Maybach, and AMG models, and this car right here is one of them.
However, the selling dealer tells those who might be interested in going home with this luxury sedan: "Mercedes has no remedy at the moment, and they have not issued a stop driving order." There is actually a remedy for it.
Photo: Bring a Trailer According to Part 573 Safety Recall Report 26V638, filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), an authorized Mercedes-Benz dealership will replace the brake hoses on the front axle on the affected vehicles.

Image: Teck Resources
Red Dog Mine in Alaska burns about 40,000 gallons of diesel a day to keep one of the world’s largest zinc mines running, and now, an 8.8-megawatt (MW) solar farm and battery storage will help cut that fuel use.
The Alaska Energy Authority’s board unanimously approved a nearly $5 million loan for the project through its Power Project Fund. Tugliq Red Dog1 will build, own, and operate the roughly $35 million solar project and sell the electricity to mine operator Teck Alaska. The state’s loan review says site work began in June and expects the solar and storage to come online in October 2028.
Red Dog sits about 105 miles north of the Arctic Circle, on land owned by NANA, an Iñupiat-owned Alaska Native corporation. The array would be larger than any solar farm operating in Alaska today, as KOTZ’s Desiree Hagen reported for Alaska Public Media. Hagen reported that the plans call for more than 15,000 panels across around 30 acres.
What will happen when the mine closes
The mine gets all its power from on-site diesel generators. In summer, it can draw so much electricity that Teck has to cut power elsewhere at the site. The solar array and the 8.8 MW, 15 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery will give the operator another source of power during those crunches.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The state of Alaska expects the solar and storage project to cover about 5% of the zinc mine’s electricity needs under its current operating plan. The project could do even more after mining ends, covering about 90% of the site’s annual electricity needs.
Teck expects the mine’s existing deposits to support operations through 2031, and it’s studying whether to develop two nearby deposits. If that expansion goes ahead, the state projects the solar and battery project would cover about 3% of the larger operation’s electricity needs. If mining ends, demand will drop sharply, but the site will still need electricity for cleanup and long-term water treatment.

EICMA 2026 • Honda CRF1150L Africa Twin Enduro Sports Is a Tongue Twister, Weighs Less but Offers More
Jay Leno Drives the Corvette That Fooled Millions as a Ferrari on Miami Vice
14 photos
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube
The Ferrari that Sonny Crockett, played by Don Johnson, drove during the first two seasons of Miami Vice was actually a replica of a 1972 Ferrari Daytona Spyder built on the chassis of a C3 Chevrolet Corvette. The man who built it has just parked it in Jay Leno's Garage.
Back in the early 1980s, kit car builder Tom McBurnie visited Newport Beach exotic car dealer Al Mardikian to discuss building Shelby Cobra replicas. After Mardikian passed on his price, McBurnie spotted a white 1972 Ferrari Daytona Spyder sitting in the showroom on consignment.
He quietly borrowed the car for a year to pull fiberglass molds from its body without the owner ever finding out. Then, he spent months reshaping the proportions to fit the C3 Chevy Corvette chassis.
After Mardikian displayed a finished replica at the Balboa Bay Club, word reached Miami Vice creator Michael Mann, who immediately wanted it as Sonny Crockett’s car. So Tom McBurnie's replica, a black fiberglass conversion, stood in for an authentic Daytona Spyder.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Real Ferrari Daytonas were extremely rare and expensive in the 1980s. Besides, Ferrari North America turned down Miami Vice because of a strict company policy against loaning or donating cars for television productions.
The production team went for the replica built on the third-generation Corvette chassis, with the first show cars using 1976 and 1981 models. Adapting the shape of the Ferrari Daytona to the chassis of the C3 Corvette required major bodywork changes, including a fiberglass body with a black plexiglass nose section.
Tom McBurnie resorted to that technical solution because the real Daytona had a 94.5-inch (2,400-millimeter) wheelbase versus the 98 inches (2,489 millimeters) that the C3 Corvette sat on, along with narrower doors and a narrower windshield.
The cabin of the Corvette was restyled to resemble that of a Ferrari. It was upgraded with tan Connolly leather upholstery and black Wilton wool carpeting, though it retained high-backed Corvette seats rather than the real Daytona’s lower seats with separate headrests.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Visible door handles with integrated keyholes held their ground, while the Daytonas had hidden handles and separate door locks. The rear bodywork was far flatter than the original sloping rear end of the authentic Ferrari.
All the time, Tom kept in touch with the stunt men of the TV series. The stunt team added a second brake pedal in the driver’s footwell, which controlled only the rear brakes, allowing stunt drivers to lock up the rear wheels on command while keeping the front wheels free to steer.
To keep the illusion alive on screen, the Miami Vice sound editors stripped out the Corvette's raw production audio during driving scenes and replaced it with post-production dubs of a genuine Ferrari V12.
For Season 2, McBurnie’s replicas were further refined. They came with a smoother front end, tinted headlight covers, repositioned Ferrari badges, and matching windshield trim. However, no matter how hard they tried, Ferrari didn't like it.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Ferrari pushed back against the replica cars in the series and took legal action over trademark infringement and look-alikes. The Italian house eventually offered to supply two 1986 Ferrari Testarossas on the condition that the fake Daytonas be retired.
The producers agreed and wrote the swap into the series. In the Season 3 premiere, When Irish Eyes Are Crying, Sonny Crockett’s black Daytona was destroyed by a Stinger missile, clearing the way for a white Testarossa to become his new signature ride. The car wasn’t really destroyed. It now sits, looking shiny and new, in Jay Leno's Garage as a guest.
This is what he takes for a spin around Los Angeles to check out how the 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) V8 behaves years after its stint in Miami. It has 180 horsepower (182 metric horsepower) on tap, but no Miami Vice clothes and soundtrack available. Still, with Tom in the passenger seat, they look like retired undercover detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo "Rico" Tubbs.
A third Daytona replica was in the making by custom car fabricator and kit-car builder Carl Roberts, but the project was dropped when the Testarossa deal went through. One of the replicas in the TV series went to a private collector, while the stunt car later appeared in the 1989 film Speed Zone and was restored for display at the Volo Auto Museum.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Now, one of those cars is parked in Jay Leno ’s Garage. It was brought there by the man who built it. Tom McBurnie tells the story of the Ferrari-wannabe Corvette. He also recalls how Ferrari did everything they could to put him out of business.
Miami Vice turned McBurnie's Daytona Spyder into a sensation, and his business simply exploded from a tiny operation with part-time employees into a 55-person affair, selling dozens of turnkey cars and hundreds of body kits. He would not sell Ferrari badges, but owners of the conversion cars bought the prancing horse logos themselves and slapped them onto the front of their vehicles.
This was seen by Ferrari as a major threat to its brand exclusivity, and they went after him in every way possible. They claimed ownership of the model’s shape and sued McBurnie Coachcraft in federal court under the Lanham Act for infringing its trade dress, arguing that the Daytona Spyder's silhouette was so "unique and distinctive" that copying it alone violated Ferrari's intellectual property.
McBurnie argued his replicas were like art lithographs that only boosted the real Daytona's fame and value. And he wasn't wrong. Real Ferrari Daytona prices on the used car market jumped from roughly $100,000 - $150,000 before Miami Vice to over $1.5 million in a couple of years.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Michael Mann testified in McBurnie’s favor, making clear that Miami Vice specifically wanted the replica for production practicality and never confused it with a factory Ferrari. Still, McBurnie had to pay his own attorneys, depositions, and court costs over several years of fighting Ferrari in federal court, costing him a total of $640,000.
On April 28, 1989, a fire devastated Tom McBurnie's shop in Santee, California, severely damaging the building and destroying multiple vehicles inside. A month later, a federal court injunction legally banned him from making Daytona replicas, which, combined with the legal bills and the fire, ended McBurnie Coachcraft’s story and put Tom McBurnie out of business.

BMW’s All-New M4 Cabrio Breaks Digital Cover, Shows Neue Klasse Electric Design in Fresh Renderings
6 photos
Photo: Kolesa
The brand-new BMW i3 is getting a Touring version , which will be a more family-oriented proposal, and a cabriolet is also in the making as we speak.
It should be called the i4 Convertible, to absolutely no one’s surprise, and it’s not a rumor, as it is indeed in the making as we speak. In fact, we spotted its range-topping full-blown M sibling recently as it was undergoing testing in the open. Yep, that would be the M4 Convertible Electric, or whatever it will be called, and it featured the usual trippy vinyl stickers on the outside, as well as a black ragtop that was not lowered in front of the camera.
Mind you, it was this exact vehicle that was used as a blank canvas by Kolesa’s Nikita Chuyko for their latest set of renderings. The first-ever battery-electric BMW M4 Convertible features a front fascia similar to the one of the new-gen i3 Sedan, save for the usual M influences. For instance, the grille is different, and the daytime running lights feature a yellow look, just like the ones of the G50 BMW 3 Series in the current range-topping flavor known as the M350 xDrive.
Photo: Kolesa If you look further down, then you will see a very familiar-looking bumper, complete with extra lights (fog lamps) on the sides, as well as two large air intakes in the middle separated by a vertical slat, and a splitter. And these were inspired by the BMW M Concept Neue Klasse, in case you forgot, just like the vented front hood, and the rear bumper, which features reflectors with a design similar to that of the front fog lamps.
The wheels haven’t been borrowed from the scooped tester this time around, but from BMW M’s portfolio. The car features a blue finish, some black details, and a black power-operated soft top that stows away in a special compartment at the rear. The cockpit should be identical to that of the new-gen i3 Sedan , as well as other Neue Klasse models, and it will include the same dashboard setup, complete with the Panoramic iDrive, and the free-floating infotainment screen.
Look for a pair of bucket seats at the front, a dedicated steering wheel and a special gear selector, new upholstery and trim, and likely different submenus and loading screens with an emphasis on the model’s full-blown M nature. Power will be shared with the upcoming BMW M3 Electric , which is understood to launch with 700 or 800 horsepower or so from its quad-motor setup that’s supposedly fed by a battery pack with a capacity of around 100 kWh.
We don’t know when the BMW M4 Convertible Electric will premiere, but it might launch around 2028, and when it does, it should look pretty much the same as the rendered one. Do you fancy the design?

EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
FedEx Driver Finds Plymouth Road Runner Rotting in Yard, It Was the 1970 Hemi 4-Speed Pilot Car
75 photos
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews
“These are my keeper cars and ones that I just uh have a lot of meaning for me and I'm going to keep for as long as I can.” To say that Dale Mathews is a car collector is like saying rain is wet. The Lenoir, North Carolina Moparhead is a larger-than-life car addict (do you have a better word?), and his collection includes some really impressive machines with equally amazing stories.
While most Mopar collectors lose sleep chasing numbers-matching hardware, Dale owns an Alpine White 1970 Plymouth Road Runner whose factory parts break every rule in the restoration manual. Featured on the Cars Over Coffee episode from the Cherries Media YouTube channel, chassis RM21R0A100015 is not a botched backyard mashup.
It is the documented one-of-one 1970 Hemi Road Runner Pilot Car—the very first 1970 Road Runner coupe Plymouth ever assembled.
Its resurrection began in 1999 when Mathews' friend, FedEx driver Ken Lewis, spotted a battered blue shell languishing in a local yard and dialed Mathews with news of a real 1970 Hemi car. Following a divorce, the previous owner had hauled off the rusty, windshield-less body while leaving scattered components behind in his former basement, and its original engine had vanished decades earlier.
Photo: YouTube/Road Test TV Crucially, the dash VIN tag, body numbers, and badly rust-cancer corroded fender tag reading PILOT survived intact. The seller already knew he possessed a rare bird—having secured a 1991 verification letter from Mopar registrar Galen Govier—and initially refused to part with it. Not the one to back down or take “No” for a definitive answer, Mathews visited repeatedly before planting a firm $6,000 offer in the man's mind at a time when local buyers might have floated $1,500, and called it “generous.”
When cash grew tight, the phone rang, and Mathews immediately trailered his rusted prize down to an Atlanta Mopar show so Govier could inspect it firsthand. Decoding RM21R0A100015 reveals a fascinating pre-production timeline straight from Detroit's Lynch Road plant. Its fender tag carries Sales Bank order number M04101 and a scheduled production date of August 1, 1969.
While that was the official opening day of 1970 model-year assembly, multiple March 1969 date codes stamped into the original glass and seat belts prove engineers hand-built it around April 1969. Even more astonishing, Govier concluded with 99% certainty that Mathews' car is the exact coupe photographed for Chrysler's September 1969 press release.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Teardown and restoration by Hodge Restorations of Inman, South Carolina exposed a forensic wonderland proving this hand-crafted mule bridged two model years. Built atop a 1969 B-body unibody wrapped in 1970 exterior sheetmetal, the chassis was never factory-dipped; workers hand-painted Alpine White across the entire undercarriage, cowl, package tray, and roof.
Its hood emblem opening was cut round, its hood lacked front-trim holes, and it carried a Dodge Charger or Coronet radiator support—complete with three latch-tray studs—stamped with its Plymouth VIN.
Every corner revealed experimental fingerprints that regular assembly-line workers never saw. The firewall retained the 1969 Air Grabber cable hole location instead of 1970 vacuum-hose routing, while 1969 inner fenders featured mounting provisions for both 1969 and 1970 battery trays. Opening the trunk exposes unique prototype reinforcement braces stamped with part number 000 that never reached production, alongside added taillight-panel brackets.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Inside, its untouched 1969 sweep-style speedometer dash and glovebox badge make it the sole known 1970 Road Runner lacking round Rallye gauges. Optioned like a pure street-strip assassin, the Alpine White post coupe wears black vinyl bench-seat trim, code M2X9, body-colored steel wheels with dog-dish hubcaps, and Goodyear Polyglas GT tires.
Under the functional Air Grabber hood thunders a dual-quad 426 Street Hemi rated at 425 horsepower and 490 lb-ft of torque, feeding an A-833 4-speed and Dana 60 axle via what may be the first Hurst Pistol Grip shifter ever fitted. Former detective and MCACN head judge Frank Badalson personally authenticated every clue ahead of its 2024 MCACN unveiling.
That no-frills, maximum-velocity ethos captured the exact spirit that birthed the Road Runner moniker just two model years earlier. By 1967, American muscle cars like Pontiac's GTO and Plymouth's own plush GTX had bloated in weight and price, pricing out young blue-collar buyers. Product planner Jack Smith and designer Gordon Cherry pitched a stripped-down, sub-$3,000 Belvedere street brawler built for 14-second quarter-miles.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Chrysler paid Warner Bros. $50,000 for the cartoon bird's rights and spent $10,000 crafting its iconic Beep Beep horn. Debuting for 1968 with a heavy-duty suspension and a standard 335-horsepower 383 V8 borrowing big-valve heads and camshaft hardware from the 440, the Road Runner detonated showroom projections. Plymouth hoped to sell 20,000 cars yet moved 44,313 units in its rookie season, including 1,009 Hemi-powered beasts.
Adding a convertible, optional Air Grabber hood, and the ferocious mid-year 440 Six-Barrel pushed 1969 volume to an all-time record of 84,420 worldwide deliveries—81,125 domestic—and earned Motor Trend's prestigious Car of the Year crown.
Refreshed front and rear sheetmetal, high-back seats, wild High-Impact hues, and the Pistol Grip shifter made 1970 the visual peak of first-generation Road Runner aggression. Nevertheless, punishing muscle-car insurance surcharges and friendly fire from Plymouth's bargain-priced compact Duster 340 slashed production nearly in half to 41,484 worldwide units, representing 36,861 American deliveries, excluding the 1,935 NASCAR-homologated Superbirds.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews 1970 also marked the final curtain for both the rigid pillared coupe body style and the open-air convertible.
Even amid inflation, Plymouth fought hard to defend its budget-muscle roots on 1970 window stickers. The stripped RM21 two-door pillared coupe—the exact configuration of Mathews' Pilot Car—started at just $2,896, while the pillarless RM23 hardtop opened at $3,034 and the RM27 convertible listed at $3,289.
Stepping up from the standard 335-horsepower 383 Road Runner V8 to the 390-horsepower 440 Six-Barrel added $250, whereas ordering the legendary 426 Street Hemi demanded an eye-watering $841 before mandatory Track Pak drivetrain and suspension upgrades.
Photo: YouTube/Cherries Media Among domestic market deliveries, 34,894 Road Runners carried the standard-issue 383—including 14,057 coupes with 5,839 manual 4-speeds—while 1,815 packed the 440 Six-Barrel (1,130 hardtops, 651 coupes, and 34 convertibles). Just 152 received the 426 Hemi: 75 hardtops (59 manuals and 16 automatics), 74 coupes (44 manuals and 30 automatics), and three convertibles, one manual and two autos.
Following that 1970 climax, emissions choke-holds and fuel crises steadily eroded the Road Runner's ferocious bite over its remaining decade. Second-generation fuselage B-bodies slumped to 13,664 units in 1971—the Hemi's swansong with just 55 built—7,628 in 1972, a brief rebound to 19,056 in 1973, and 11,355 in 1974.
After 7,183 Fury-based hardtops closed its standalone B-body run in 1975, the badge shrank into a compact Volaré trim package from 1976 through 1980, sliding from 8,769 in 1976 and 6,975 in 1977 to 1,357 in 1978 and just 496 final 318-powered cars in 1980.
Photo: Facebook/Dale Mathews Standing at the very headwaters of 1970 production as the first of 44 Hemi 4-speed coupes—and the lone factory prototype linking 1969 and 1970—RM21R0A100015 belongs in a museum wing. Yet Mathews rejects static velvet-rope ownership, regularly rowing that historic Pistol Grip shifter across North Carolina backroads just to feel the synchros engage.
Saved from a rusty yard for a stratospheric $6,000, Plymouth's primal 1970 Road Runner still runs fast, loud, and fiercely alive exactly as Detroit built it to run.

Dealer Selling Nice Dodge Challenger SRT Hellcat, Muscle Car Costs a Lot Less Than a New Charger
20 photos
Photo: Instagram | automotive_ambitions
Can we interest you in a Dodge Challenger SRT Hellcat ? You probably said yes. After all, you are now here, reading these lines and looking to find out whether the example pictured below is worth your time, and, better said, your hard-earned money.
If you are indeed in the market for such a model, then you know that these are on the affordable side of things today. That is if you aim for an older model year, as these tend to go for roughly 40,000 in today’s market. Sure, paying that sum would get you a high-mileage example, most of the time, whereas for roughly $15,000 to $20,000 more, you’d get a later model year car with fewer miles, whereas $75,000 or so would get you a barely driven example that’s much newer.
On a six-digit budget, the superior Dodge Challenger SRT Demon 170 becomes available, as this one now sells for between $100,000 and close to $150,000. And as a quick reminder, it remains the fastest and most powerful production muscle car ever. Beat that Ford and Chevrolet! And Dodge, too, for that matter. No, seriously, Dodge, please beat that, because the automotive world needs another neck-snappingly fast muscle car, and you’re the undisputed king when it comes to these!
Photo: Instagram | automotive_ambitions Mind you, we are not here to talk about a possible spiritual successor to the mighty Demon 170, nor to remind you that Ford is still the only company that offers V8-powered muscle cars, nor to refresh your memory about the fact that the Chevrolet Camaro is dead. For now, anyway. Instead, we should put the spotlight on the vehicle pictured in the gallery, which, as mentioned above, is looking for a new home, and it is a US-registered car, with a clean title.
According to the listing, the ride in question is a 2016 model year Dodge Challenger SRT Hellcat , presented in white with golden wheels, red brake calipers, plenty of black details, and tinted windows. It features a red and black interior, remote engine start, a power sunroof, Laguna Performance Seats, and a few other things that are mentioned in the ad. As for the odometer, it read 57,000 miles (~91,700 km) or so at the time of cataloging.
Power is supplied by none other than the 6.2-liter supercharged V8 Hellcat lump. The unit was good for 707 hp (717 ps/527 kW) and 650 lb-ft (881 Nm) of torque when the car was new, and everything goes to the rear axle via an eight-speed automatic transmission. From 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph), this model needed a little over three and a half seconds, and the top speed was 199 mph (320 kph).
As for the how much it costs part of the story, you are looking at $43,991. That’s less than a new Charger, as mentioned in the title, which has an MSRP of $49,995. View this post on Instagram A post shared by AUTOMOTIVE AMBITIONS (@automotive_ambitions)

Hyundai isn’t just giving its compact SUV a fresh coat of paint. The next Kona is getting a major overhaul, and now we’ve caught an early glimpse of the N Line variant.
Hyundai’s new Kona gets the N Line treatment
The Kona is getting an upgrade. Hyundai launched the second-generation Kona in 2023, so like most of its vehicles, a mid-cycle refresh is due around next year.
Apparently, that won’t be the case. Hyundai appears to be skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh for the third-generation Kona, with plans for a complete redesign.
Several disguised test vehicles have been spotted over the past few months in the US, Europe, and South Korea with a noticeably different design. The test mules sit higher off the ground and have a much more commanding, SUV-like shape, close to the new Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Two versions have been captured thus far: a standard Kona and a more rugged XRT variant. For the first time, the new Kona N Line was spotted in Korea by HealerTV on a car carrier.
Since it’s still covered and an early-stage prototype, it’s hard to see many changes outside of the exclusive wheels and the added lower side skirt.
The new Kona N-Line is expected to receive other exclusive N Line design elements, including a more aggressive, sporty front and rear design with unique bumpers.
Hyundai second-generation Kona Electric N Line (Source: Hyundai)
The early prototype sighting suggests Hyundai is keeping the N Line trim in the third-gen Kona lineup.
Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona Electric in the US but said it would return for the 2027 model year, when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.
Like the current generation, the new Kona is expected to be available in gas, hybrid, and fully electric powertrains. It’s expected to debut in 2027 as a 2028 model year. Earlier this month, a prototype was captured in Korea that was expected to be the EV version ( see the images here ).
